catalog_quote: Tataltepec Chatino and the other languages of Core Chatino (Zenzontepec Chatino and all extant topolects of Eastern Chatino) all share this stem-final stress where disyllabic stems ω are realized as σW σS.1 ... [fn. 1] The opposite pattern of stem-initial stress (where disyllabic ω are realized as σS σW) is present in the non-Core Chatino Zapotecan languages, including the now-extinct Soltec and arguably the extinct Teojomulco Chatino (Sullivant, under review).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Soltec is said to have had stem-initial stress: in a disyllabic stem the first syllable was stressed and the second unstressed (σS σW), the opposite of the stem-final stress of Core Chatino. This is inferred by Sullivant from the 1886 Peñafiel wordlist (the only data), and the footnote defers the argument to Sullivant (under review) = Sullivant 2016, IJAL 82(4), which could not be opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the language is extinct and known only from a 250-item wordlist, so no statement about exceptions exists.
new_statements.domain_note: Stem-level (disyllabic stem ω); nothing said about clitics, phrases or citation forms for Soltec. Statement is a footnote in a description of a different language (Tataltepec Chatino), i.e. a second-hand report of the author's own unpublished-at-the-time analysis. No accent is marked in the Mechling 1912 published portion of the wordlist.
new_statements.identity_note: Soltec/Solteco = the extinct language of San Miguel Sola (Sola de Vega area), Oaxaca (Glottolog solt1234, no ISO code), attested only in Peñafiel's 1886 wordlist; distinct from the living Zapotec varieties of the Sola de Vega region. The stress claim in Sullivant 2015 concerns this extinct language, grouped there with Teojomulco Chatino (teoj1234) as 'non-Core Chatino Zapotecan languages' with σS σW stems.

sources.quote: Linguistically, Soltec is the earliest Zapotec language to diverge from the rest (Smith Stark 2007). Philological evidence indicates that it may not have participated in a change that shifted prominence from the ultima of some words to the penult.
sources.note: Hedged ('may not have participated'), based on philological (colonial-era) evidence; the language is dormant. Implies Soltec kept final (ultima) prominence in words where other Zapotec shifted to the penult. Footnote 13 (p. 32): no tonal data available for Soltec.

sources.quote: The opposite pattern of stem-initial stress (where disyllabic ω are realized as σS σW) is present in the non-Core Chatino Zapotecan languages, including the now-extinct Soltec and arguably the extinct Teojomulco Chatino (Sullivant, under review).
sources.note: Fn. 1, p. 55 (section 2.2.1, on Tataltepec Chatino stem-final stress): 'The opposite pattern of stem-initial stress (where disyllabic ω are realized as σS σW) is present in the non-Core Chatino Zapotecan languages, including the now-extinct Soltec and arguably the extinct Teojomulco Chatino (Sullivant, under review).' Also fn. 17: Soltec shows traces of Proto-Zapotecan vowel nasalization (Peñafiel 1886; Smith Stark 1999). The claim about Soltec defers to Sullivant (under review) = Sullivant 2016 IJAL.

The only accent remarks in the paper concern Amuzgo pitch accent (p. 665) and Pochutla Nahuatl (p. 681).

Nothing; Solteco only listed in Smith Stark 2007's Western Zapotec branch.
